title: A new concept of frequency-excitation-up conversion to improve the yield of linear piezoelectric generators

sections.heading: A new concept of frequency-excitation-up conversion to improve the yield of linear piezoelectric generators
sections.text:
W. Chen a,b, J.L. Mo a,b,∗, Z.Y. Xiang a,b, A.Y. Wang a,b, Q.A. Liu a,b, H.H. Qian a,b

a Tribology Research Institute, School of Mechanical Engineering, Southwest Jiaotong University, Sichuan, Chengdu, 610031, China b Technology and Equipment of Rail Transit Operation and Maintenance Key Laboratory of Sichuan Province, Sichuan, Chengdu, 610031, China

Received in revised form 12 March 2021   
Accepted 19 March 2021   
Available online 23 March 2021

Keywords:   
Energy harvesting   
Frequency-excitation-up-conversion   
Ultra-low frequency   
Friction nonlinearities

A new and novel frequency-excitation up-conversion (FEUC) mechanism achieved by converting lowfrequency excitation into friction-induced vibration (FIV) is proposed to improve the output power of linear piezoelectric energy harvesters at ultra-low ambient frequencies. For comparison, a conventional resonant energy harvester and an impact-driven energy harvester are created, the output power is measured at the resonant frequency under a $0 . 5 ~ \mathrm { g }$ driving acceleration. Then, a friction system driven by reciprocating sliding and capable of generating FIV is established. The driving reciprocating is equivalent to the low-frequency ambient vibration, and a single piezoelectric cantilever beam is added to the friction system for energy recovery. The results show that, compared with the impact-driven energy harvester, the vibration frequency can be increased hundreds of times, and the excitation level can be improved several orders of magnitude by the friction nonlinearities. The impedance of the energy harvester is reduced significantly due to a sharp increase in the vibration frequency. In addition, the open-circuit voltage amplitude is not substantially lowered due to the significantly increased excitation level, even though the piezoelectric cantilever beam operates in a high-frequency condition and in the absence of resonance. Therefore, the output power is dramatically improved. The effectiveness and superiority of the FEUC strategy proposed in this work has been demonstrated.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Energy harvesting is a trending topic due to the strong emphasis on low-carbon technologies and environmental protection in recent decades. In particular, with the increased use of low power consumption electronics, such as sensor networks used in monitoring applications and micro-electro-mechanical systems (MEMS), harvesting ambient vibration energy has become a promising research topic to provide sustainable power supply for these types of electronics [1–5]. Several vibration energy conversion mechanisms have shown promise, i.e., electromagnetic [1], electrostatic [2], piezoelectric [3], magnetostrictive [4], and triboelectric mechanisms [5]. Piezoelectric energy harvesting is a preferred technology owing to its properties of simple structure, high power density, and easy to applicate and has been extensively studied [3,6].

Generally, a conventional piezoelectric energy harvester is a cantilever beam stacked with a piezoelectric layer and held by a vibrator that provides sustaining excitation for electric energy generation from bending deformation of the piezoelectric layer [7]. However, this type of design is a linear approach that only works effectively at the resonant frequency of the structure. Both experimental and analytical studies have demonstrated that once the working frequency shifts away from the resonant frequency of the energy harvester, even slightly, a significant reduction in the harvested power will occur [7–9]. Nevertheless, the ambient vibration is broadband and has a wide spectrum range, and most importantly, it is random [9–11]. These properties of ambient vibration inevitably result in obstacles to linear energy harvesting in practical applications [10].

Typically, most ambient vibrations are characterized by a large amplitude and low frequency [12]. For example, the frequency of human motion is general $2 - 3 \ \mathrm { H z }$ , wave motions are ${ < } 1 \ \mathrm { \textrm { H z } }$ , vehicle vibrations are ${ < } 2 0 \ \mathrm { H z }$ , and construction or mechanical equipment vibrations are ${ < } 1 0 \mathrm { H z }$ [13–15]. It is generally difficult to harvest energy from such low-frequency and low-intensity vibration sources. To operate efficiently in these cases, the resonant frequency of the energy harvester must be lowered to achieve frequency matching. However, this strategy complicates the structural design and weakens the strength of the energy harvester since a tip mass and increasingly compliant springs are needed [16]. This configuration is not suitable in cases where bulk consumption and displacement are limited. Another problem is that lead zirconate titanate (PZT) or piezoelectric ceramic material is fragile, and large deformation is not possible [16–18].

It has been theoretically demonstrated that the power yield of the vibration energy oscillator is positively correlated with the vibration frequency [19]. Consequently, Frequency up-conversion (FUC) mechanisms that can bridge the gap between high-frequency resonance and low-frequency excitation have been proposed to allow energy harvesters to operate efficiently at low frequencies and broaden their bandwidth [13,15,16,19–21]. Many authors have reported on prototypes that exploit FUC for low-frequency vibration energy harvesting. Wu [15] et al. proposed a FUC mechanism based on a binder clip structure; the device utilizes the basic characteristics of spring pendulums to scavenge ultra-low frequency vibration energy efficiently. Han [22] et al. proposed a modified FUC technique to reduce the threshold level of excitation acceleration for energy harvesters based on the snap-through buckling principle. Gu [16] et al. and Chen [23] et al. achieved FUC using an impact. Apart from linear approaches, nonlinear methods or a combination of the two strategies have also received attention but are rarely reported. For instance, Wang [19] et al. presented their models and experiments of a piezoelectric energy harvester, in which FUC is induced by the combined effect of magnetic nonlinearities and mechanical piecewise linearity. Their device can boost the output power by 35 times and uses almost half the operational frequency threshold compared to the conventional counterparts. In essence, most of the reported FUC techniques are resonant and impactdriven, in which high-frequency generating beams and flexible driving beams are required. The basic mechanism can be described as follows: the flexible driving beam is first excited by base acceleration and resonates at low frequency. Following an impact between the driving beam and the generating beam, both beams vibrate together for a short period and then they vibrate separately. Meanwhile, the generating beam, which is activated by the instantaneous impact, will vibrate feely at the higher natural frequency after the separation and simultaneously generates high-frequency voltage signals. However, a frequency-matching strategy is indispensable in these approaches since the driving beam needs to resonate at the low excitation frequency; thus, the operating bandwidth of the energy harvester is still narrow since such technique is essentially based on linear resonance. Moreover, the structures become more complicated and require more space as additional cantilever beams are introduced.

Another common but generally neglected and harmful vibration source in our surroundings is friction-induced vibration (FIV). Typically, FIV is a self-excitation phenomenon resulting from frictional nonlinearities at the sliding contact between two solid surfaces [24–26]; FIV does not rely on any external excitations. The vibration frequency is mostly determined by the inherent properties of the friction systems (such as the stiffness and mass) [26–28]. In most cases, FIV arising from mode-coupling or lock-in instability scenarios can lead to high-frequency and high-intensity vibrations, generating sustained and stable acoustic emissions during sliding at the contact interfaces [29,30]. Therefore, FIV is a potential vibration source that can overcome frequency mismatching and provide significant power output. Recently, piezoelectric energy harvesting using FIV has received increasing attention. Tadokoro [31] et al. experimentally and numerically investigated piezoelectric energy harvesting via stick-slip motion by using a single-degreeof-freedom friction system. Helseth [32] studied the feasibility and characteristics of piezoelectric and triboelectric energy harvesting from stick-slip motion. Chen [33] et al. achieved FIV suppression and energy harvesting from FIV by combining piezoelectric elements with elastic damping components. FIV energy harvesting is an emerging research field with new developments in recent years. However, most reported works have focused only on the fundamental understandings of this topic.

Chehami [29] et al. recently reported that the low-frequency ambient vibrations can be converted into high-frequency FIV through frictional contact nonlinearities, although the purpose is for passive defect detection and localization in structures instead of vibration energy harvesting. Inspired by this, we propose a nonimpact, non-resonant frequency-excitation up-conversion (FEUC) mechanism that uses friction nonlinearities to transfer energy from primary low-frequency ambient excitation to a secondary converted FIV field at high frequencies. Compared with the conventional resonant-impact-driven FUC strategy, the working frequency and the excitation level is increased by several orders of magnitude due to the high-frequency and high-intensity properties of FIV. As a result, the impedance of the piezoelectric patch is reduced, and the open-circuit voltage amplitude is maintained although the resonance is not considered; thus, the output power of the energy harvester is significantly increased. Moreover, this approach does not require the modification of the structure of the energy harvester, and no magnets or any other additional cantilever beams are needed. The results of this study provide a new energy harvesting approach from ultra-low frequency ambient vibration.

sections.heading: 2.1.1. Methodology
sections.text: Two conventional vibration energy harvesters are created, the first one is a resonant energy harvester, as shown in Fig. 1 (a), it is a cantilever beam $( 5 0 ~ \mathrm { m m } \times 1 6 ~ \mathrm { m m } \times 0 . 3 ~ \mathrm { m m } )$ stacked a piezoelectric layer $1 7 \mathrm { m m } \times 1 6 \mathrm { m m } \times 0 . 2 5 \mathrm { m m } )$ ) on the root. To operate efficiently at low vibration frequencies, a lump mass of $_ { 4 0 \ g }$ $3 0 \ : m m$ $\times ~ 1 0 ~ m m { \times } 1 8 ~ m m )$ is mounted at the end of the cantilever beam to lower its natural frequency to match the $2 0 H z$ excitation frequency. Fig. 1(b) shows the impact-driven energy harvester, two stoppers are introduced to induce impact between the tip mass and the stoppers, where frequency-up conversion can be achieved. At the start the vibrator locates in its initial position, the stopper is positioned 0.5 mm away from the cantilever beam. When the vibrator moves to its ending position, there is another stopper 0.5 mm away from the ending position. The two stoppers are symmetrically arranged about the equilibrium point of the vibrator so that the energy harvester can generate a steady voltage signal. Both energy harvesters are driven by a 0.51 $\mathrm { g } ( 5 \mathrm { m } / s ^ { 2 } )$ sinusoidal acceleration and resonate at $2 0 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ .

sections.heading: 2.1.2. Results and discussion
sections.text:
The electric power output (the mean energy delivered within a second) and the peak-to-peak voltage against the load resistance of the two energy harvesters are shown in Fig. 2. The results show that, for both energy harvesters, as the load resistance increases, the voltage increases at a decelerating rate initially and ultimately converges to a limit value. It can be found that the peak to peak voltage is significantly improved after introducing stoppers, owing to the larger strain in the piezoelectric layer caused by the instantaneous impact-induced nonlinearity effect. The power delivered to the load first increases and then decreases with the increase in the resistance. An optimal power output of approximately $6 \mu \mathrm { W }$ is obtained at the matched resistance for the resonant energy harvester, yielding the maximum power delivery to the load resistance. While the impact-driven energy harvester yields a maximum power of $3 0 \mu \mathrm { W }$ , five times larger than that of the previous one. One can note that the optimal resistance of the impact harvester is smaller than that of the resonant energy harvester, which is due to the up converted frequency. Generally, the piezoelectric energy harvester can be simply modeled as an equivalent electric circuit with a voltage source connected in series to a free capacitor due to its capacitive nature (known as RC matching) [34,36]. The optimal load resistance is thus regarded as the impedance of the piezoelectric capacitor, which can be approximated as $1 / C \omega$ , where C and $\omega$ are the equivalent piezoelectric capacitance and angular frequency of the voltage, respectively. Thus, the optimal load resistance decreases with the increase of the working frequency. The RC matching strategy has been extensively used in both analytical models and experiments owing to its satisfactory accuracy in most cases [34–36].

sections.heading: 2.2.1. Test setup and methodologies
sections.text:
The test setup to implement the proposed FEUC mechanism is shown in Fig. 3. The device consists of a loading cell, a fixture, a friction pad, a flat specimen, and a vibrator that provides harmonic excitation. Since the energy harvester will work under high-frequency conditions, the tip mass of the piezoelectric cantilever beam is removed. The fixture that holds the friction pad is bolted on the loading cell. The flat specimen is mounted on the vibrator. When the test starts, a normal load of $2 0 \ \mathrm { N }$ is applied on the loading cell so that the friction pad attached to the fixture can establish close contact with the flat specimen. Afterward, the vibrator starts to reciprocate in sine motion at a set stroke and frequency. The flat specimen glued on the vibrator will rub against the friction pad and generate high-intensity FIV due to the relative movement between the two components, and the converted FIV is then used to excite the piezoelectric cantilever beam to generate electric power.

In this study, four different reciprocating frequencies with a consistent stroke of $1 0 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ are used to operate the vibrator. The reciprocating frequencies are 2, 3, 4, and $5 \mathrm { H z }$ , and the corresponding equivalent excitation accelerations are 0.79, 1.78, 3.16, and 4.93 $\mathrm { m } / { \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 } }$ , respectively. The vibration and voltage signals at the different reciprocating frequencies are obtained by a digital acquisition system for conducting a comparative analysis. Each test lasts $6 0 s$ and is repeated three times to ensure good repeatability and reliability of the results.

![](images/f65195d83b2126ea66bcd4fd78076947391c2a0c56ed8c158077fe75970dde9b.jpg)  
Fig. 3. Schematic of the test setup.

sections.heading: 2.2.2. Results and discussion
sections.text:
The vibration acceleration and open-circuit voltage signals at different reciprocating frequencies are shown in Fig. 4. The experimental results show that in general, unstable vibrations only occur in the first half stroke of the reciprocating process, and correspondingly a high-frequency oscillating voltage signal is generated. In addition, it is found that the amplitude value of the FIV acceleration is almost $1 2 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m } / s ^ { 2 }$ , which is much larger than that of the primary excitation acceleration (less than $5 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 } .$ ). Thus, the intensity of the vibration acceleration has increased significantly after the secondary conversion via the friction nonlinearities. Generally, if the resonant frequency of an oscillator increases, the amplitude at resonance will decrease at the same level of excitation. However, an increase in the excitation level compensates for the reduction in the dynamical response. Therefore, the open-circuit voltage amplitude of the FIV field is comparable to that of the impact energy harvester, although frequency-matching was not the objective. It is also found that the reciprocating frequency has a negligible influence on the FIV intensity, resulting in a relatively small difference in the voltage amplitude.

![](images/258e263b75004852d79441ce1fe6e6e53b33203403275d36ff8f369c44232456.jpg)  
Fig. 4. (a) Acceleration of FIV at different reciprocating frequencies and (b) the corresponding output voltage.

Fig. 5 shows the frequency spectrum of the vibration acceleration and the output voltage at different reciprocating frequencies. The vibration and voltage signals have identical fundamental frequencies $3 0 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ , $5 1 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ , etc.), indicating that the piezoelectric voltage is induced by the FIV. Note that the frequencies of the FIV are much larger than those of the primary excitation (i.e., the reciprocating frequencies), demonstrating that the proposed FUC strategy is highly effective. More importantly, the frequency spectrum of the unstable vibration is marginally affected by the reciprocating frequency, which is in line with the results of the reviewed studies discussed in the introduction. Hence, FIV can be considered a potential approach to deal with the narrow bandwidth of linear energy harvesters and extend the operational bandwidth to ultralow frequencies.

The peak-to-peak voltage across the load and the mean power delivered to the load as a function of the load resistance at different reciprocating frequencies are shown in Fig. 6. Similar to the results in Fig. 2, with the increase in the load resistance, the amplitude of the voltage gradually increases and then stabilizes, whereas the output power first increases and then decreases. The output power at a reciprocating frequency of $2 \ \mathrm { H z }$ is smaller than those at the other three reciprocating frequencies, which is responsible for the short unstable vibration interval of the friction system at this reciprocating frequency, as can be seen in Fig. 4. Nevertheless, compared with the results in Fig. 2, the power harvested from the secondary converted FIV field is several times larger than that generated by the resonant impact energy harvester. Moreover, the primary excitation level used here (less than $5 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 } .$ is lower than that of the low-frequency excitation used in the first control experiment $( 5 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { { s } } ^ { 2 } )$ . These results indicate that a superior output power can be produced by exploiting frictional nonlinearities even if a vulnerable driving source is applied. The superiority of the proposed energy harvesting approach from low-frequency ambient vibrations has been demonstrated. Besides, due to the high-frequency property of the FIV, the optimal resistance here is sharply reduced to $1 5 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ , which is an order magnitude smaller than those of the resonant energy harvester and the impact energy harvester. Consequently, the output power is significantly improved compared with the conventional impact-driven FUC strategy.

sections.heading: 3.1. Complex eigenvalue analysis
sections.text:
Finite element analysis has been widely adopted to study FIV in recent years in addition to experimental studies. Two methodologies are typically available in finite element analysis for interpreting frictional phenomena, namely, dynamic transient analysis and complex eigenvalue analysis [28,37–39]. The dynamic transient analysis allows for solving the dynamic response of the friction systems directly in the time domain by considering the nonlinear aspect of frictional contact; the displacement, velocities, acceleration, and forces during the friction process can be determined. However, transient analysis is computationally complex, that’s because, the finite element kinematic equations are numerically solved by explicit or implicit integration rules. In contrast, complex eigenvalue analysis detects the instability of the friction system by analyzing its eigenvalues and eigenvectors; thus, the computational complexity is lower. The eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the governing equation may be complex because of the asymmetry of the stiffness matrix due to the friction terms. The imaginary part $\left( I _ { m } \right)$ of the eigenvalue represents the FIV frequency, and the real part $\left( R _ { e } \right)$ is the growth rate of the unstable vibration. Once the real part becomes positive, the system is likely to be unstable [28]. The propensity of the instability is evaluated by the parameter of effective damping ratio, which is written as $\begin{array} { r } { \varepsilon = { - } \frac { 2 R _ { e } } { I _ { m } } } \end{array}$ 2Re . A smaller value of $\varepsilon$ indicates a greater tendency of the friction system to generate FIV [28,38,40]. In this study, complex eigenvalue analysis is conducted to predict the unstable frequencies of FIV generated in the experiment, as well as the unstable modes at these frequencies, demonstrate the feasibility of energy harvesting by FIV, and investigate the effect of critical parameters, such as the friction coefficient on the piezoelectric power generation. Detailed information on performing complex eigenvalue analysis in the commercial finite element software ABAQUS can be referred to other published papers [33,37,41]. ![](images/f46c97e3d27aff709495a01964cd1fa1b013a7060544a749a3fe45c07a9498b6.jpg) Fig. 5. The finite element model of the friction system is established in ABAQUS and is shown in Fig. 7(a). The numerical model is created based on the real test rig, which consists of a loading cell, a fixture, a friction pad, a flat specimen, a vibrator, and a cantilever beam. The material properties used in this model are set according to the actual values of the components in the test rig; the details are listed in Table 1. The load and boundary conditions of the numerical model are shown in Fig. 7(b). The upper surface of the loading cell is constrained in all degrees of freedom, except for the translation degree of freedom in the z-direction. A normal load of $2 0 \mathrm { N }$ is applied on the upper surface of the loading cell to press the friction pad onto the flat specimen. A frictional contact is defined at the contact interface between the friction pad and the flat specimen, the contact formulation at the sliding interface is defined as small sliding with a penalty method, in which Coulomb’s friction law is used to govern the frictional dynamic behavior. The bottom of the vibrator is fixed in the z- and y-directions; a velocity boundary condition is applied in the $\mathbf { x } .$ -direction. Threaded and glued connections are set as a tie constraint to minimize the computational complexity. To ensure a good reliability of the finite element model and determine the mesh size, a grid convergence work is performed. A primary model with a coarse mesh is constructed, using this model to calculate the normal force and tangential force at the contact interface. Then the overall mesh size is reduced, and particularly, the contact interface, that is the most important part determining the computational accuracy of the finite element model, is specially treated with refined mesh. The mesh optimization is not completed until the mesh size does not affect the calculation results of the interfacial forces. The convergent computational results are then compared with the experimental results to estimate the reliability of the optimized finite element model. Finally, the mesh size is determined, which is the presented form showing in Fig.7. A total of 37,236 C3D8 brick elements are generated in the finite element model. A single analysis requires a few minutes on a PC. Fig. 8 (a) shows the imaginary parts (frequency) of the complex eigenvalue versus the friction coefficient. Two mode coalescences are observed; the $4 ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ and $5 ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ mode first start to coalesce at $5 7 9 . 1 \mathrm { H z }$ when $\mu = 0 . 1 5$ , and subsequently, the $2 ^ { \mathrm { n d } }$ and $3 ^ { \mathrm { r d } }$ mode coalesce at $2 9 9 . 2 2 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ when $\mu$ further increases to 0.33. It is noteworthy that the coalesced frequency of the $4 ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ and $5 ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ mode decreases with an increase in the friction coefficient. The threshold value of the friction coefficient under this mode coalescence is very small; thus, the result is unlikely for a metal counterface, and the corresponding unstable frequency is unreliable. The real friction coefficient obtained from the experiment is 0.65, at which the unstable frequency is $5 0 5 . 7 7 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ , which is very close to the experimental dominant frequency of $5 1 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ . The error percentage is only $0 . 8 3 \ \%$ However, the friction coefficient has no visible effect on the coalesced frequency of the $2 ^ { \mathrm { n d } }$ and $3 ^ { \mathrm { r d } }$ mode. The unstable frequency is $3 0 6 . 8 4 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ at the experimental friction coefficient, coinciding with one of the experimental results of $3 0 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ . One should note that not all the unstable frequencies in the experiment have been detected by the complex eigenvalue analysis, the reason is that complex eigenvalue is a linearized analytical method, in which nonlinear aspect of frictional contact is not considered. Therefore, some of the unstable frequencies of FIV can be either overestimated or underestimated by the complex eigenvalue analysis. Nevertheless, the complex eigenvalue analysis can still provide us an in-depth understanding on FIV and energy harvesting via FIV [33]. The effective damping ratios of the $3 ^ { \mathrm { r d } }$ and $5 ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ mode are shown in Fig. 8 (b). Similarly, once the friction coefficient exceeds the critical value, a negative damping ratio is observed, suggesting that the friction system tends to generate FIV. Moreover, the damping ratio becomes smaller with an increase in the friction coefficient, indicating that the unstable vibration is more likely to occur in the high friction coefficient range; a higher friction coefficient intensifies the unstable vibration of the friction system. Therefore, a large friction coefficient is desirable in FIV energy harvesting. ![](images/daba78b55f8fb54f7ff27207c7f3cf5b07b1d38e691d0ce1e6cdc81fe8db3d03.jpg) Fig. 7. (a)The finite element model of the test setup; (b) the generated mesh and boundary conditions of the numerical model. ![](images/a8bad8992ca58a712291a91ff1f138c0d8f6269a9b5a572e8d0bc7c894cd3edc.jpg) Fig. 8. Frequency of the unstable mode (a), and effective damping ratios of the friction system (b) versus friction coefficient. The unstable mode shape of $3 0 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ is shown in Fig. 9(a). This mode shape is manifested as the bending deformation of the fixture, which is in line with the fact that the friction force at the contact interface drags the fixture when the vibrator translates in the x-direction. In particular, the cantilever beam shows significant bending movement in the x-direction, indicating that it will deform in the $\mathbf { x }$ -direction, thus converting vibration energy into electric energy. Likewise, the unstable mode shape of $5 0 5 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ also shows visible bending deformation in the fixture and the cantilever beam (Fig. 9(b)). Due to the higher order of vibration, the mode shape is more complex than that of the lower order, and additional deformation is occurring in the loading cell. The results indicate that the unstable FIV is composed of multiple vibration patterns, which complicates the frequency spectrum of the FIV and the piezoelectric voltage signal. Thus, the complex eigenvalue analysis demonstrates the feasibility of energy harvesting via FIV. In addition, by calculating the unstable frequency and unstable mode shape, we obtain deep insights into the complex vibration pattern of the friction system, which may be of great significance in designing the structure of an FIV energy harvester.

sections.heading: 3.2.1. Analyzing of a linear energy generator
sections.text:
The simplified model of a linear piezoelectric energy harvester used for the analysis is shown in Fig. 10 [42]. The dynamical model of the vibration-based energy harvester can be regarded as a singledegree-of-freedom mass-spring-damper system attached to a base, which provides an incentive displacement y. The lumped mass is forced to vibrate to produce a relative displacement $z$ between the mass and the base, and the vibration energy is thus converted into electric energy due to the direct piezoelectric effect. According to Newton’s law and Kirchhoff’s law, the governing equations of the electromechanical system are expressed as:

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { m \ddot { z } + c _ { p } \dot { z } + k _ { p } z + \alpha U = - m \ddot { y } } } \\ { { \qquad } } \\ { { \alpha \dot { z } - C \dot { U } - \cfrac { U } { R } = 0 } } \end{array}
$$

where $m , c _ { p }$ , and $k _ { p }$ are the effective mass, damping, and stiffness of the cantilever beam, respectively. $\alpha$ represents the equivalent electrometric coupling coefficient; $C$ is the equivalent capacitance of the piezoelectric material; $R$ is the external load resistance; $U$ is the voltage across the load resistance.

![](images/557ede6188aee9c92b09fc672822a17a9d1f072aab80973b5661a1aaed402ef5.jpg)  
Fig. 9. Unstable mode shape of $3 0 0 \mathrm { H z }$ (a) and unstable mode shape of 505 Hz (b).

![](images/9b303eb41bf4dfe357d5905795eaa9df0c55bb9c488f355fde0694bd6868f07d.jpg)  
Fig. 10. Simplified model of a linear piezoelectric energy harvester.

Since the given harmonic excitation is kept constant, the vibration of the oscillator and the damping effect of the piezoelectric energy generation do not affect the input base acceleration. Thus, the dynamical response of the oscillator and the voltage signal will also be harmonic and possess the same frequency as the base acceleration. For simplicity, we assume that the relative displacement of the mass is:

$$
Z = \mathsf { A s i n } ( \omega t )
$$

where A is the amplitude of the relative displacement of the mass, and $\omega$ is the circular frequency of the base acceleration. Substituting Eq. (2) into Eq. (1) provides the output voltage:

$$
U = U _ { 0 } e ^ { - \frac { t } { R C } } + \frac { A \alpha } { C } \sqrt { 1 - \frac { 1 } { 1 + \left( R C \omega \right) ^ { 2 } } } \mathrm { s i n } ( \omega t + \varphi )
$$

Where

$$
\mathrm { t a n } \varphi = { \frac { 1 } { R C } }
$$

The first term in Eq. (3), which depends on the electrical initial condition, will decay to zero within a short period of time. The steady response of the voltage signal is the second term. It can be found that the voltage response has the same frequency as the base acceleration. With the increase in the load resistance, the amplitude of the output voltage gradually increases at first and then infinitely approaches but never reaches the limit value of $\frac { A \alpha } { C }$ as the load resistance rises to infinity, i.e. the open circuit voltage is $\textstyle { \frac { A \alpha } { C } }$ . The power delivered to the load resistance can be derived from Eq. (3):

![](images/8e5488aee86c30c3c2c27544a5ab9435d6c3c29ab699c5849bce8bfcc8b44306.jpg)  
Fig. 11. The power delivered to the optimum load resistance versus the excitation frequency for different base accelerations.

$$
P = { \frac { ( A \alpha ) ^ { 2 } } { 2 \left( { \frac { 1 } { R \omega ^ { 2 } } } + R C ^ { 2 } \right) } }
$$

Thus, the output power reaches the peak value when $R { = } 1 / \omega C$ :

$$
P _ { m a x } = \frac { A ^ { 2 } \alpha ^ { 2 } \omega } { 4 C }
$$

The theoretical predictions coincide with the RC matching. Moreover, Eq. (6) shows that the delivered maximum power is proportional to the frequency of the base acceleration and the square of the displacement amplitude, which means that the optimal output power will increase if the excitation frequency increases and meanwhile the vibration amplitude of the energy generator is maintained.

Based on Eq. 1, the simulated output power of a linear energy harvester delivered to the optimum load resistance as a function of the excitation frequency for different base accelerations is given in Fig. 11. The numerical simulation here is not intended to reproduce the results of the first control experiment in this paper, instead it means to present some basic features of linear energy harvesters. The result shows that the maximum power is generated at the resonant frequency. The performance of the energy harvester will be sharply reduced if it operates out of resonance. Generally, it is impossible for the energy harvester to operate at resonance in all cases due to the random nature of the ambient vibration, as well as the narrow bandwidth of the linear vibrator. However, the vibrator is extremely sensitive to the excitation intensity, i.e., an increase in the base acceleration can lead to a significant increase in the harvested energy. This result means that the energy loss caused by frequency mismatching can be compensated for by increasing the base acceleration if it is possible to obtain high-intensity excitation.

sections.heading: 3.2.2. Modeling of energy harvesting from FIV
sections.text:
A detailed finite element model of the test setup (Fig. 3) is able to provide the results of the displacement, forces, and many other relevant factors through transient analysis. However, the simulation of frictional contact at the interface (a non-smooth dynamic phenomenon) of a finite element model even of moderate size has high computational requirements due to the complexity of the detailed model and the large mesh with many elements. Therefore, instead of using the finite element model, a simplified two-degreeof-freedom FIV model integrated with a linear piezoelectric energy harvester is developed to simulate piezoelectric energy harvesting via FIV combined with FUC, as shown in Fig. 12. This model is based on the minimal model adopted by many investigators to study mode coupling instabilities [43,44]. The lumped mass $M$ represents the equivalent mass of the fixture and the load cell, and $m$ is the mass of the cantilever beam. A constant normal load force $F$ is exerted on the lumped mass $M$ to achieve contact with the rigid belt; both components are linked by a linear spring $K _ { 1 }$ and a cubic spring $K _ { n l }$ . The rigid belt reciprocates in a sinusoidal rhythm at a certain frequency equivalent to the reciprocating movement of the vibrator. A Coulomb-type friction law is assumed to govern the friction between the rigid belt and M. An oblique spring $K _ { 3 }$ , which inclines at an angle of $1 3 5 ^ { \circ }$ to the horizontal direction, is included to couple the horizontal vibration with the vertical vibration of $M$ . In addition, $M$ is constrained by a spring in the horizontal direction. A viscous damper is installed in the vertical or horizontal direction; its coefficients are $C _ { 1 }$ and $C _ { 2 }$ , respectively. In the horizontal direction, a linear piezoelectric generator is attached to $M$ with a spring $K _ { p }$ and a viscous damper $C _ { p }$ . The effective mass of the generator is m. Dry friction is produced at the sliding contact when the rigid belt starts to move, inducing unstable vibration of $M$ . The energy generator that is excited by the horizontal vibration of $M$ , is forced to vibrate and generates electricity. The coupled equation of the piezoelectric-friction system is expressed as: $$ \left\{ \begin{array} { l l } { \displaystyle M \tilde { x } + ( c _ { 2 } + c _ { p } ) \tilde { x } - c _ { p } \dot { x } _ { p } + ( K _ { 2 } + K _ { p } + \frac { K _ { 3 } } { 2 } ) x + } \\ { \displaystyle \left( \mu K _ { 1 } - \frac { K _ { 3 } } { 2 } \right) y - K _ { p } x _ { p } - \alpha U + \mu K _ { n } y ^ { 3 } = 0 } \\ { \displaystyle M \tilde { y } + C _ { 1 } y + ( K _ { 1 } + \frac { K _ { 3 } } { 2 } ) y - \frac { K _ { 3 } } { 2 } x + K _ { n } y ^ { 3 } = - F } \\ { \displaystyle m \tilde { z } + C _ { p } \tilde { z } + K _ { p } z + \alpha U = - m \tilde { x } } \\ { \displaystyle \alpha \tilde { z } - C \dot { U } - \frac { U } { R } = 0 } \\ { \displaystyle z = x _ { p } - x } \end{array} \right. $$ Due to the reciprocating motion of the rigid belt, the direction of the friction force alternates at the rhythm of the reciprocating motion of the rigid belt. Therefore, a constant friction coefficient is not appropriate. The time history of the displacement of the vibrator, the friction force, and the friction coefficient obtained from the experiment are shown in Fig. 13. It can be observed that the direction of the friction force is positive in the forward stroke of the vibrator and reverses in the backward stroke. The friction coefficient, however, shows a larger value in the forward stroke and a smaller value in the backward stroke, explaining why the unstable vibration always occurs in the forward stroke of the reciprocating process. Higher friction coefficients are more likely to trigger instability of the friction system, which is in agreement with the complex analysis. In fact, the friction coefficient should be negative in the backward stroke. Here, it is treated as a scalar; therefore, no directivity is presented. However, the friction coefficient should have opposite signs in the two stroke processes when conducting numerical simulations using Eq. (7). Based on the obtained friction coefficient and the other experimental parameters (see Table 2), the vibration and voltage signals of the piezoelectric-friction system are simulated by solving Eq. (7). The reciprocating frequency is $4 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ ; the vibration and voltage signals are shown in Fig. 14. The simulation shows that, in the forward stroke, high-frequency fluctuation is observed and grows exponentially at the beginning, then decays into a limit cycle. When the rigid belt moves backward, however, the unstable vibration attenuates rapidly and soon disappears. Moreover, the voltage signal shows the same evolution as the vibration acceleration. The numerical result is highly consistent with the experimental results. Fast Fourier transform (FFT) analysis of the vibration and voltage signals provides an identical fundamental frequency of $5 1 6 \mathrm { H z }$ , which is very close to the experimental result. Note that only one unstable frequency is predicted by the numerical model. The reason is that the lumped mass $M$ only has two degrees of freedom. According to the mode-coupling theory [43], the two distinct modes of the friction system start to coalesce into a single one as the friction coefficient increases to the critical value. As a result, the instability of the friction system is triggered. Therefore, only one distinct vibration frequency is detected by the numerical model. Another fact lies in that, friction-induced vibration is an extremely complicated phenomenon, which is not only determined by the stiffness and damping factors, but also determined by interfacial properties, for example, the contact plateaus, wear debris and surface roughness of the sliding interface [38,40,45]. It is impossible to incorporate all these details in a minimal numerical model. Thus, there are some differences between the simulation results and the experimental results. Nevertheless, by choosing reasonable parameters, this numerical model can well simulate the vibration manner of the experiment friction system. Furthermore, it can also precisely predict the intensity and the fundamental frequency of the unstable vibration. Therefore, this numerical model is able to capture some basic features of the experiment system, which can be adopted in studying energy harvesting via friction-induced vibration. (a) The limit cycle for different load resistance values and (b) the output power versus the load resistance. As discussed in Section 3.2.1, if the external load resistance does not suppress the intensity of FIV, i.e., the damping effect of piezoelectric power generation does not affect the limit cycles, and the curves of the voltage across the load and the delivered power versus the load resistance are similar to those in Fig. 6. The limit cycles of the friction system for different load resistances are shown in Fig. 15 (a). The load resistance has a negligible effect on the dynamical response of the friction system. The simulated output power as a function of the load at different reciprocating frequencies is shown in Fig. 15 (b). The simulated value of $R _ { o p t }$ is very close to the experimental result, which demonstrates the reliability of the numerical model and indicates that the selected system parameters are reasonable. However, the simulated power is slightly higher than the experimental result. The discrepancy between the experimental and numerical results may be attributed to the simplification of this model since only a single stable limit cycle is calculated. Under real conditions, the amplitude of the vibration fluctuates significantly due to the rich dynamic response, resulting in more “blank” during the unstable vibration interval. The integral energy is thus smaller than the numerical result.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusion
sections.text: A new and novel energy transfer concept from ultra-low frequency vibrations to the secondary high-frequency FIV field using contact friction nonlinearities was proposed for effective harvesting of vibration energy at ultra-low ambient frequencies. By exploiting dry reciprocating friction, the vibration frequency was increased hundreds of times, and the excitation level was enhanced several orders of magnitude; the proposed mechanism is referred to as the FEUC mechanism. Compared to the conventional impactdriven FUC strategy used in energy harvesting from ultra-low frequencies, the impedance of the piezoelectric generator was significantly lowered, and the amplitude of the open-circuit voltage was nearly maintained in the new approach. Thus, the harvested power was increased several times even though a vulnerable excitation acceleration was adopted. More importantly, the frequency of FIV was nearly unaffected by the low-frequency external excitation, indicating that the operating bandwidth of the energy harvester can be broadened to ultra-low frequencies. Complex eigenvalue analysis demonstrated the feasibility of energy harvesting via FIV. The unstable vibration frequencies of FIV were accurately predicted, and the corresponding unstable vibration patterns were obtained. The analysis indicated that the friction coefficient is a crucial factor in FIV energy harvesting; a larger friction coefficient results in more vibration energy, which is beneficial for piezoelectric energy harvesting via FIV. A low-order theoretical model was established based on the real physical parameters of the test rig and could capture the basic features of the FEUC mechanism. The results of this work showed that the maximum output power delivered from the secondary FIV field was several times larger than that generated by the conventional impact-driven energy harvester, even though the impact-driven system operated at resonance. This result indicates that the new energy harvesting concept is highly effective for vibrations with low frequency and low intensity.
